Day 71 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Architecture

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

Kubernetes is a set of cooperating control-plane and node components that continuously reconcile declared state into running workloads.

Architecture / mental model

kubectl/clients → kube-apiserver → etcd
                         ↓
                 scheduler/controllers
                         ↓
                worker node: kubelet → runtime → Pods

How it works

The API server is the front door to the control plane. Clients submit and read Kubernetes API objects through it, while etcd persists API state.

The scheduler watches for Pods that need a node and selects a suitable placement. Controllers continuously compare desired and observed state and request changes when they differ.

On workers, kubelet ensures Pod specifications are realized through a supported container runtime. Service networking is implemented by the cluster's data-plane components; the published architecture introduced kube-proxy as the node rule manager.

Hands-on reference

kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

Verification

Inspect cluster and node state, then create a disposable workload and follow the object from API creation to scheduling and a running Pod. Do not infer control-plane health from one working `kubectl get` alone.

Field note / gotcha

Kubernetes is not one giant container manager. Each component owns a different part of the reconciliation path, so 'Kubernetes is broken' is not yet a diagnosis.

Security considerations

The API server, etcd and kubelet are high-value boundaries. Strong authentication/authorization, protected etcd access and secured node APIs matter because compromise can become cluster-wide.

What I learned

Troubleshooting improves when you know which component owns the decision you are questioning.
